item.statement_excerpt:
Assume Countable Choice. Fix a compact smooth Riemannian target $(X,g)$, a compact half-dimensional submanifold $L$, a smooth complex structure $J_b$ on $TX|_L$ for which $L$ is totally real, and an angular length $T>0$. Let $J(\sigma,\tau,x)$ be smooth almost complex structures on $[a,b]\times[0,T]\times X$, with uniform bounds for $J$ and its first two target covariant derivatives, and with $J(\sigma,0,x)=J(\sigma,T,x)=J_b(x)$ for $x\in L$. There are constants $\varepsilon,c,C>0$, independent of $a,b$, such that every smooth solution
$$u_\sigma+J(\sigma,\tau,u)u_\tau=0,\qquad u(\sigma,0),u(\sigma,T)\in L,$$
with $\sup|du|_g+\sup(|\partial_\sigma J|+|\partial_\tau J|)\le\varepsilon$ satisfies
$$E_g(u;[a+R,b-R]\times[0,T])\le C\varepsilon^2e^{-cR}\qquad(0\le R\le(b-a)/2).$$
In particular central energies vanish uniformly with the distance $R$ from the ends of these long boundary necks. Both angular edges lie on the same $L$; this is not a statement about strips with two different boundary submanifolds.

proof_step_donor_fragments.exact_current_text: A fixed finite-atlas embedding is obtained as follows. Choose a finite smooth partition $\phi_i$ with compact supports in coordinate charts $x_i$, using finite Euclidean bumps and normalization, and set $F(x)=(\phi_i(x),\phi_i(x)x_i(x))_i$. Equality of these coordinates recovers $x$ in a chart where $\phi_i>0$, and vanishing of their derivatives recovers a zero tangent vector in that chart. Thus $F$ is injective and immersive, and compactness makes it an embedding. Derivatives of $F$ are bounded and its differential uniformly compares $g$ with the ambient Euclidean metric. Write $Y=F(X)$ and $M=F(L)$. [given, construct, algebra]

We construct a smooth involution $\rho$ on a neighborhood of $L$ in $X$, fixing $L$, whose differential is $+I$ on $TL$ and $-I$ on $J_bTL$. First the ambient normal map $(y,n)\mapsto y+n$ from the Euclidean orthogonal normal bundle of $Y$ has invertible differential along its zero section. By [F3] it has local smooth inverses. It is injective for a uniform small normal radius: otherwise collisions with normal vectors tending to zero have base points converging after a subsequence by compactness; equality of images forces the same base limit, contradicting the local inverse there. The same compactness argument preserves invertible differential on a uniform radius. Projection of these glued inverses to $Y$ gives a smooth ambient retraction $P$ near $Y$ with $dP$ the tangent projection along $Y$. Now on the vector bundle $N_y=dF(J_bT_xL)$ over $y=F(x)\in M$, consider $\Phi(y,v)=P(y+v)\in Y$. At $v=0$ its derivative identifies $T_yM\oplus N_y$ with $T_yY$, since $L$ is totally real. The identical local-inverse and compactness argument gives a diffeomorphism from a uniform small symmetric bundle neighborhood onto a neighborhood of $M$ in $Y$. Conjugating $(y,v)\mapsto(y,-v)$ by this diffeomorphism and then by $F$ defines $\rho$. It is an involution, fixes $L$, and has the claimed differential. On a smaller fixed neighborhood all its first and second derivatives, and its inverse differential, are bounded. [F3, step 1.1, construct, algebra]

For small enough $\varepsilon$, the entire map lies in that fixed neighborhood: each path $\tau\mapsto u(\sigma,\tau)$ begins on $L$ and has length at most $T\varepsilon$. Define on the doubled angular circle of period $2T$ $$\widetilde u(\sigma,\tau)=\begin{cases}u(\sigma,\tau),&0\le\tau\le T,\\ \rho(u(\sigma,-\tau)),&-T\le\tau\le0,\end{cases}$$ identifying $-T$ and $T$. This is $C^1$ across both seams. Values agree because $\rho$ fixes $L$. Tangential derivatives agree because $u_\sigma\in TL$ there, so $d\rho u_\sigma=u_\sigma$. The equation gives $u_\tau=J_bu_\sigma\in J_bTL$, so the normal reflected derivative $-d\rho u_\tau$ equals $u_\tau$. These identities hold along the whole seam and may also be differentiated in $\sigma$. Thus all tangential derivatives of the values and normal first derivatives match. The doubled map is smooth on each closed side. [step 2.1, given, construct, algebra]

Put $V=F\circ\widetilde u$ and let $H=\Delta V$ weakly on the doubled cylinder. There is no line measure in this Laplacian because $V$ and its first derivatives match across the seams; integrating by parts on both sides verifies cancellation. On the original half, the composition formula and [F1] bound $|H|\le C(|du|_g^2+\kappa|du|_g)$. On the reflected half the composition rule for $F\circ\rho$ gives the same bound, with a larger fixed constant from its second derivatives. The equation gives $|du|_g\le C|u_\tau|_g$, and the embedding and reflected inverse differential compare this with $|V_\tau|$ on either side. Hence $$|H|\le C_0\varepsilon|V_\tau|$$ almost everywhere on the entire doubled cylinder. This argument does not assume a globally smooth reflected almost complex coefficient across a seam. [F1, step 1.1, step 2.1, step 3.1, algebra]

Set $w=V_\tau$ and $e(\sigma)=\tfrac12\int_{-T}^T|w|^2d\tau$. The function $w$ is continuous and piecewise smooth, its angular derivative is an ordinary bounded piecewise function locally, and it has zero angular mean. Moreover $\Delta w=\partial_\tau H$ as distributions. Tangential differentiation of the piecewise formulas gives $$e''=\int_{-T}^T\bigl(|w_\sigma|^2+|w_\tau|^2-\langle w_\tau,H\rangle\bigr)d\tau.$$ For completeness the last integration by parts is distributional: $w$ is periodic $H^1$ in its angular variable and $H\in L^2$, so convolution on that circle proves $\langle\partial_\tau H,w\rangle=-\int\langle H,w_\tau\rangle$ by passage to the $L^2$ limit. Thus any jumps of $H$ are included, and no angular endpoint term was omitted. The matching tangential derivatives from step 3.1 justify differentiating the integral twice in $\sigma$. [step 3.1, step 4.1, construct, algebra]

Young's inequality and [F2] give, for $\lambda=(\pi/T)^2$, $$e''\ge\tfrac12\int|w_\tau|^2-\tfrac12C_0^2\varepsilon^2\int|w|^2\ge\tfrac12(\lambda-C_0^2\varepsilon^2)\int|w|^2.$$ Decrease $\varepsilon$ so that $C_0^2\varepsilon^2\le\lambda/2$ and set $c=\sqrt{\lambda/2}$. Then $e''\ge c^2e$. The barrier $h=e(a)e^{-c(\sigma-a)}+e(b)e^{-c(b-\sigma)}$ has $h''=c^2h$ and dominates the endpoint values of $e$. A positive interior maximum of $e-h$ would contradict $(e-h)''\ge c^2(e-h)$, so $e\le h$. Its integral on $[a+R,b-R]$ is at most $c^{-1}(e(a)+e(b))e^{-cR}$. [F2, step 4.1, step 5.1, construct, algebra]

The original energy is bounded by $C\int e(\sigma)d\sigma$, by the original equation and embedding norm equivalence. The small derivative hypothesis and the fixed reflected derivative bound give $e(a)+e(b)\le C\varepsilon^2$. Substitution in step 6.1 proves the asserted central energy estimate with a uniform constant. This proves boundary neck decay using the actual totally real boundary geometry. It does not address two different submanifolds or construct a bubble-tree decomposition. [step 1.1, step 2.1, step 3.1, step 6.1, algebra] ∎

proof_route: Finite-atlas embedding and finite-dimensional inverse collars construct reflection rho with derivative +TL/-JTL. Small gradient confines halfloops to collar. Actual reflected map is C1 across periodic seams, so ambient Laplacian has no line atoms and satisfies quadratic tension bound piecewise. Distributional angular integration includes jumps of H; periodic Wirtinger and maximum principle give exponential energy decay.
